questions.q: Your support agent has an intake subagent that classifies incoming requests (simple: tracking/password/status | complex: refund/damage/billing), and an investigation subagent that handles complex cases. The intake subagent correctly marks requests as "simple" about 85% of the time, but 40% of requests marked simple still reach the investigation subagent, adding unnecessary latency. The system prompt says "skip investigation for simple cases," but logs show it's ignored. What's the most reliable fix?
options: Increase the intake classification model's temperature to make decisions more decisive
Add a step in the coordinator that reads the intake classification and only invokes the investigation subagent for cases marked complex
Include 5 few-shot examples in the intake prompt showing requests classified as simple
Increase the token budget for the intake subagent so it has more confidence in its decisions
questions.explain:
A system-prompt instruction ("skip investigation for simple cases") provides only probabilistic compliance. The reliable fix is a deterministic gate in the coordinator that simply never invokes the investigation subagent for cases the intake subagent already marked simple, enforcing the decision at the control-flow level instead of hoping the model follows a prose instruction.
Not “Increase the intake classification model's temperature to make deci…” — Temperature affects randomness in sampling, not whether a downstream step respects the classification. Investigation would still run for cases marked simple whenever the coordinator invokes it.
Not “Include 5 few-shot examples in the intake prompt showing requests c…” — Few-shot examples may sharpen classification, but the classification is already mostly right. The failure is that the result is ignored when deciding whether to invoke investigation.
Not “Increase the token budget for the intake subagent so it has more co…” — A bigger token budget gives the intake subagent room, not authority. The 40% leak happens after classification, where a control-flow check is missing.

questions.q: Your process_refund and request_refund_exception tools have descriptions: "Process a refund" and "Request an exception for refund eligibility." Both accept the same inputs (order_id, amount, reason). The agent calls the wrong one 25% of the time on policy-edge cases. You've already tried improving the descriptions with input formats, but misrouting persists. What's the next step on the fix ladder?
options: Add 8 few-shot examples showing correct tool selection for ambiguous cases
Rename request_refund_exception to escalate_refund_exception_review and add explicit "use this when policy does NOT allow the refund" guidance
Merge both tools into one and add an internal action: "approve" | "request_exception" input parameter
Split the tools into separate subagents, each with their own tool, to eliminate the choice entirely
questions.explain:
Once description improvements alone haven't resolved misrouting, renaming the ambiguous tool to make its purpose unmistakable — escalate_refund_exception_review, with explicit "use this when policy does NOT allow the refund" guidance — is the next rung on the fix ladder, ahead of merging tools with an internal parameter or splitting into separate subagents, both more disruptive changes.
Not “Add 8 few-shot examples showing correct tool selection for ambiguou…” — Examples are a later lever, and the tools take identical inputs and still sound alike. Fixing the naming and the "when policy does not allow" trigger is the cheaper next step.
Not “Merge both tools into one and add an internal `action: "approve" | …” — Merging both tools behind an internal action parameter is a more disruptive redesign that moves the same ambiguity into a parameter value instead of clarifying it.
Not “Split the tools into separate subagents, each with their own tool, …” — Splitting into separate subagents is a heavy architectural change. The next step is to make the exception tool's name and purpose unmistakable.

questions.q: After 12 turns investigating a disputed charge, your agent has verified the customer, retrieved three years of billing history, and identified the root issue ($200 overcharge on order #7743 from March). But when asked to "process the refund," it hesitates and asks "just to confirm, the order with the issue was...?" instead of recalling the specific order number. What's the problem, and how should it be fixed?
options: The model's context window is too small; increase it to preserve history better
Extract a persistent "case facts" block containing critical details (customer ID, order number, issue amount, dates) that's carried separately from the narrative conversation history
Reduce the number of turns allowed before summarization
Require the customer to re-state the order number before proceeding
questions.explain:
This is context loss in a long investigation: specific numbers and identifiers can fade from a narrative history even though the conversation is nominally still "about" the same case. A persistent case-facts block (customer ID, order number, amount, dates) carried separately from the narrative is the direct fix — more targeted than simply enlarging the context window or asking the customer to repeat themselves.
Not “The model's context window is too small; increase it to preserve hi…” — A larger window does not stop specific identifiers fading from a narrative history. The details need to be stored somewhere they cannot get lost.
Not “Reduce the number of turns allowed before summarization” — Summarising sooner would compress detail earlier and make the loss of the order number and amount more likely, not less.
Not “Require the customer to re-state the order number before proceeding” — Asking the customer to repeat the order number pushes the system's memory failure onto them and does not fix the underlying context loss.

questions.q: You've split the support system into a coordinator plus two subagents: one for order investigation and one for risk assessment. A case arrives: "I want a $500 refund due to damaged goods." Both subagents run, but the coordinator receives only risk-assessment findings ("Low risk, proceed") and no findings from the order-investigation subagent. Production logs show the order-investigation subagent ran but hit a backend timeout. The coordinator can't distinguish "no issues found" from "investigation failed," so it proceeds with incomplete information. What change would best solve this?
options: Restructure the case so order investigation always runs first, and risk assessment only if investigation succeeds
Require both subagents to output a status field indicating success/failure/partial, plus structured error context (errorCategory, isRetryable) when something goes wrong
Merge the two subagents into one
Add a retry loop in the coordinator that automatically re-invokes failed subagents
questions.explain:
When a subagent fails, the coordinator needs a structured signal to tell "nothing was found" apart from "the investigation itself failed." A status field (success/failure/partial) plus structured error context (errorCategory, isRetryable) gives the coordinator exactly that distinction; without it, a silent timeout can look identical to a clean negative result.
Not “Restructure the case so order investigation always runs first, and …” — Running investigation first still would not tell the coordinator whether it succeeded. A silent timeout would remain indistinguishable from a clean result.
Not “Merge the two subagents into one” — Merging the subagents does not fix the missing failure signal. A single agent could still hide a timeout behind a silent empty result.
Not “Add a retry loop in the coordinator that automatically re-invokes f…” — Automatic retries do not tell the coordinator what happened when retries fail, and they would not separate a clean negative from a failure.

questions.q: The MCP backend exposes tools that list available refund policies, approved return-reason codes, escalation-queue names, and supported regions. In production, every new case triggers 4 discovery tool calls to learn what exists, consuming roughly 800ms of latency before any customer-specific lookup happens. These lists change weekly but are read-only. Logs show the agent burns token budget on discovery before it can act. What's the most appropriate integration change?
options: Cache the tool outputs in a CLAUDE.md file so the agent reads them once
Expose these catalogs as MCP **resources** (URI-addressable reference data) rather than **tools**, so the agent can read them directly without consuming a model decision or a round-trip
Create a single get_system_metadata tool that returns all four catalogs at once
Require the agent to skip discovery entirely and rely on its training knowledge of policies
questions.explain:
Read-only, rarely-changing catalogs that exist to be discovered rather than acted upon belong in MCP resources, not tools — removing the round-trip decision cost entirely. Caching in CLAUDE.md still requires re-reading the catalogs into context every session, and merging into a single tool still costs a round-trip.
Not “Cache the tool outputs in a CLAUDE.md file so the agent reads the…” — A CLAUDE.md copy still must be loaded into context each session and goes stale as the lists change weekly, and it does not remove discovery calls.
Not “Create a single get_system_metadata tool that returns all four ca…” — One combined metadata tool still costs a round trip and a model decision per case, so the latency problem is only reduced, not removed.
Not “Require the agent to skip discovery entirely and rely on its traini…” — Policy and region catalogs that change weekly cannot be reliably recalled from training knowledge, so the agent would act on outdated or invented information.

questions.q: A case is escalated to a human agent with a 72% confidence score and a note saying "case seems complex." But investigation shows: customer identity is verified, order exists, refund window is open, damage evidence is clear, and refund amount is within policy. The escalation was triggered by an engineer's "confidence < 80% → escalate" rule. The confidence actually dropped to 72% only because the agent was uncertain whether a small warehouse fee was refundable, not because the case itself was complex. What's fundamentally wrong with this escalation signal?
options: The confidence threshold is too strict; raise it to 60%
Self-reported model confidence is poorly calibrated — it correlates weakly with actual case complexity and can be confidently wrong on the easiest cases while uncertain on genuinely simple ones
Confidence scores should be averaged across the whole case, not reported per-turn
Use turn count instead of confidence; escalate after 6 turns regardless of complexity
questions.explain:
Self-reported model confidence is a poorly calibrated proxy for actual case complexity — it can dip on a single unresolved sub-question even when every other part of the case is completely clear-cut, which is exactly what happened here. Escalation thresholds built on this signal will misfire in both directions: escalating clear cases and failing to escalate genuinely hard ones.
Not “The confidence threshold is too strict; raise it to 60%” — Moving the threshold to 60% does not make confidence reflect real complexity. The 72% was caused by one small unresolved question, so the signal itself is the problem.
Not “Confidence scores should be averaged across the whole case, not rep…” — Averaging confidence over the whole case still depends on a poorly calibrated self-reported number, so it does not fix the flawed signal.
Not “Use turn count instead of confidence; escalate after 6 turns regard…” — Turn count does not measure complexity either, since routine cases can need several turns while hard ones resolve quickly.

questions.q: A customer asks, "Can you process my refund now?" The agent's response includes a tool-use block for process_refund with correct parameters, but the response text also says "I've processed your refund — you should see it in 3–5 business days." The application's agentic loop terminates after seeing this final text and never executes the pending tool call, so the customer gets a confirmation message but no refund is actually issued. What's the design flaw?
options: The model should never generate customer-facing text in the same response as a tool call

The loop must check whether stop_reason is "tool_use" to know a tool call is pending; if so, it must execute the tool and continue the loop rather than treating the response as final just because text is also present
The response should be split into two separate API calls to avoid mixing concerns
Add a deterministic check for phrases like "processed" in the text to prevent premature loop termination
questions.explain:
The agentic loop must check whether stop_reason is "tool_use" to know a tool call is still pending, and execute it regardless of any accompanying text, rather than treating the presence of customer-facing text as a signal that nothing further needs to happen. Terminating early here means the tool call that should have processed the refund never actually runs.
Not “The model should never generate customer-facing text in the same re…” — Text alongside a tool call is normal. The flaw is how the loop interprets the response, not that the model produced customer-facing text.
Not “The response should be split into two separate API calls to avoid m…” — Splitting the response into two API calls adds complexity without changing that the loop must act on a pending tool call.
Not “Add a deterministic check for phrases like "processed" in the text …” — Scanning the text for phrases like "processed" is brittle and unrelated to whether a tool call is pending. stop_reason is the reliable signal.

questions.q: Production analysis shows an inverted pattern: simple requests (resend tracking link, password reset) are escalated 35% of the time, while complex policy cases (international damage claims, subscription billing disputes) are resolved autonomously 28% of the time — both wrong outcomes. Investigation reveals the agent escalates using a heuristic: "if the conversation has more than 5 turns, escalate." But simple cases often need 6–8 turns for data gathering (a customer didn't provide an order number initially, or an email needed clarifying), while some policy cases resolve in 3–4 turns given the right expertise. Why is this heuristic unreliable, and what should replace it?
options: Use conversation length but adjust the threshold per case type; simple cases get a higher turn limit

Escalation should be based on explicit, measurable criteria — policy ambiguity in the documentation, required customer data the customer can't provide, or conflicting information from backend systems — not proxy metrics like turn count
Escalate only when the model's confidence score drops below 50%
Always escalate cases with more than 4 tool calls, since tool-call count indicates complexity
questions.explain:
Turn count is a proxy that doesn't track actual complexity — a routine case can easily need extra turns just for data-gathering, while an expert can resolve a genuinely complex policy question in very few. Escalation should trigger on explicit, checkable conditions instead: policy ambiguity, missing customer-supplied data, or contradictory backend information.
Not “Use conversation length but adjust the threshold per case type; sim…” — Adjusting turn limits per case type keeps a proxy that does not measure complexity, so simple and complex cases would still be misrouted.
Not “Escalate only when the model's confidence score drops below 50%” — A 50% confidence cut-off relies on self-reported confidence, which is poorly calibrated and would also misroute simple and complex cases.
Not “Always escalate cases with more than 4 tool calls, since tool-call …” — Tool-call count is another proxy for complexity and would again escalate routine multi-step cases while missing genuinely complex ones.

questions.q: A coordinator invokes a refund-decision subagent with a highly prescriptive prompt: "Check if customer is verified AND order exists AND refund window is open AND damage evidence is provided. If all true, approve. If any false, escalate. If customer is verified but evidence is unclear, gather more details." On standard, well-documented cases this works, but on unusual cases (a customer claims damage but has no photo, or the return window is ambiguous due to international shipping), the subagent either escalates unnecessarily or asks for details the coordinator already tried to gather. What's the architectural flaw?
options: The subagent needs the full conversation history passed explicitly

The prompt over-specifies decision steps with rigid if-then-else logic, leaving no room for the subagent to reason about nuanced cases; it should instead receive investigation tools and clear decision criteria, but be allowed to assess independently whether those criteria are met
The coordinator should call a different subagent for unusual cases
The refund-decision subagent shouldn't have access to investigation tools at all
questions.explain:
A rigid, fully-enumerated if-then-else prompt leaves the subagent no room to reason when a real case doesn't map cleanly onto the enumerated conditions (missing photo evidence, ambiguous international shipping windows). The better design gives the subagent the same investigation tools and the underlying decision criteria, but lets it assess whether those criteria are satisfied given what it can actually observe, rather than forcing an exact literal match.
Not “The subagent needs the full conversation history passed explicitly” — Passing the full history would not fix the core issue, which is that the prompt enumerates rigid conditions that unusual cases cannot match.
Not “The coordinator should call a different subagent for unusual cases” — Routing unusual cases to a different subagent does not remove the brittle if-then logic and requires predicting every unusual case in advance.
Not “The refund-decision subagent shouldn't have access to investigation…” — Removing investigation tools would leave the subagent unable to assess cases itself, which makes the over-escalation worse.

questions.q: A /refactor-tests skill encodes a company's standard test-refactoring pattern. It was originally created at ~/.claude/skills/refactor-tests/SKILL.md to test locally. Now 40 engineers need to use it consistently. What's wrong with the current location, and what's the correct migration path?
options: Personal skills are faster; keep it at the user level and have each engineer copy the file manually to their own machine

The user-level location is personal and not version-controlled; the skill should move to .claude/skills/refactor-tests/SKILL.md in the repo so every engineer inherits it via git and uses identical logic
Create a duplicate at the project level while keeping the user-level version, so team members can use either
Convert the skill into a slash command instead, since skills can't be shared across a team
questions.explain:
User-level configuration is personal and never shared through version control, no matter how good the skill is. Making a skill available consistently to 40 engineers means it has to live at the project level, where every clone of the repo inherits the identical file — not duplicated in two places or manually distributed.
Not “Personal skills are faster; keep it at the user level and have each…” — The user-level copy stays personal. Having every engineer copy it by hand is error-prone and lets versions drift, which defeats consistent use.
Not “Create a duplicate at the project level while keeping the user-leve…” — Keeping two copies invites the two versions to diverge, so engineers may end up running different logic.
Not “Convert the skill into a slash command instead, since skills can't …” — Skills can be shared across a team when placed at the project level, so converting to a slash command is unnecessary.

questions.q: A skill spawns a subagent with context: fork to explore third-party API documentation and produce a long reference document summarizing it. When control returns to the main session, the developer asks Claude to use that reference for code generation, and Claude says it has no knowledge of any such reference. What's the underlying issue?
options: context: fork writes to an isolated temporary sandbox, and any file the fork creates never exists outside it

A forked subagent's internal reasoning and any artifacts it produced are not automatically available to the parent session; whatever the fork returns as its final result must be explicitly passed back as context (or written somewhere the main session actually reads) for the main session to use it
Subagents are not permitted to produce long-form output when context: fork is set
The reference exists, but the developer must use a memory-inspection command to view fork-isolated outputs
questions.explain:
A forked subagent's internal reasoning and any artifacts it generates don't automatically flow back to the parent session — only whatever the fork explicitly returns as its result does. If the main session needs the reference material, it has to be passed back directly or written somewhere the main session actually reads, not just produced somewhere inside the fork.
Not “context: fork writes to an isolated temporary sandbox, and any fi…” — A fork is not a sandbox that destroys its output. What the fork returns can be passed back explicitly, so the gap is about transferring results, not about files vanishing.
Not “Subagents are not permitted to produce long-form output when `conte…” — Nothing limits forked subagents to short output. It could produce a long reference, but the main session still has to be handed that result.
Not “The reference exists, but the developer must use a memory-inspectio…” — No special inspection command exposes fork-isolated work to the parent. The result has to be passed back or saved where the main session reads.

questions.q: A developer is implementing a distributed caching layer in a service they've never worked with before. They ask Claude to implement it directly, with a long, detailed prompt describing the desired behavior. After review, they discover the design doesn't account for TTL-based expiry, an important pattern in that service, forcing a rework. On a second, similar task in the same unfamiliar service, they instead ask Claude to first surface open design questions before writing any code; Claude asks about TTL handling, consistency guarantees, and cache scope, all of which shape the eventual implementation. Why did this approach work better here?
options: Interviewing Claude before implementation always produces objectively better code, regardless of context

In an unfamiliar domain where the relevant tradeoffs and constraints aren't already known, surfacing design questions before coding catches gaps that a single detailed upfront prompt is likely to miss, since the prompt-writer doesn't yet know what they don't know
The interview approach is faster because it skips implementation
The interview approach forces more thorough documentation as a side effect
questions.explain:
The interview pattern earns its value specifically in unfamiliar territory, where the person writing the prompt doesn't yet know which tradeoffs matter (like TTL-based expiry here) and so can't have specified them upfront. Surfacing design questions before implementation catches exactly the kind of gap that a single detailed prompt — however thorough it feels — is likely to miss when the domain itself is the unknown.
Not “Interviewing Claude before implementation always produces objective…” — Interviewing is not always better. Its value depends on the domain being unfamiliar, so a blanket claim of better code ignores that.
Not “The interview approach is faster because it skips implementation” — Surfacing questions does not skip implementation. It happens before coding, and its payoff is catching missing design considerations, not speed.
Not “The interview approach forces more thorough documentation as a side…” — Better documentation may result, but it is not why the approach worked. The benefit was exposing the TTL and consistency considerations.

questions.q: A developer is refactoring a function signature used across 30 files and updating its 15 call sites. After 12 files, they discover the new signature breaks an edge case they hadn't planned for and need to work out a fix. Should they fork the session to explore the fix, or keep working in the main session?
options: Fork the session to explore the fix in isolation, then bring the result back into the main refactoring

Continue in the main session — it retains full context of the 12 files already changed, avoiding lost work; forking here would isolate the fix but strip away the surrounding refactoring context the fix actually needs
Restart the whole task from scratch with updated requirements
Forking is only appropriate for documentation work, never for code changes
questions.explain:
Continuing in the main session preserves the accumulated context of the 12 files already changed, which the fix genuinely depends on; forking at this point would isolate the fix into a context that's missing exactly the surrounding refactoring work it needs to stay consistent with.
Not “Fork the session to explore the fix in isolation, then bring the re…” — Forking would isolate the fix from the accumulated work on the 12 changed files, which the fix needs to remain consistent with.
Not “Restart the whole task from scratch with updated requirements” — Restarting from scratch discards the 12 files already changed and wastes that work when the main session can carry on.
Not “Forking is only appropriate for documentation work, never for code …” — Forking is not limited to documentation. It is a general tool, but here its isolation would cost context the fix depends on.

questions.q: A .claude/rules/api-validation.md file has frontmatter paths: ["src/api/**/*.ts"], containing rules about validating all API inputs. A developer creates src/api-client/index.ts — a sibling directory, not a subdirectory of src/api/ — and asks Claude to implement an API client there. The validation rules never apply to this file. Why?
options: The glob src/api/**/*.ts only matches paths under src/api/; src/api-client/ is a different directory that happens to share a name prefix, so the pattern simply doesn't match it — a broader pattern would be needed to cover both
.claude/rules/ files only apply to files that already existed when the session started
Glob patterns are case-sensitive and the path casing doesn't match
Rule paths require an exact directory match, and sibling directories are always excluded by design
questions.explain:
Glob matching is literal path matching: src/api/**/*.ts matches only paths that actually fall under src/api/, and src/api-client/ is a distinct sibling directory that happens to share a prefix, not a match for that pattern. A broader pattern (or an additional rule) would be needed to cover both directories.
Not “.claude/rules/ files only apply to files that already existed whe…” — Path-scoped rules are not limited to files that existed when the session started. The pattern simply does not match this sibling directory.
Not “Glob patterns are case-sensitive and the path casing doesn't match” — Case sensitivity is not the problem. The directory name api-client is a different path from api and not a casing mismatch.
Not “Rule paths require an exact directory match, and sibling directorie…” — Rule paths do not require an exact directory match or exclude siblings by design. A pattern matches whatever paths its glob covers, so a broader glob can include both.

questions.q: A developer spends four hours refactoring a component library. Two hours in, Claude reads and correctly restates an explicit architectural constraint: "all async operations must use Suspense; no raw promises directly in JSX." At hour four, asked to add a new async feature, Claude writes a component that awaits a promise directly inside a useEffect, violating that constraint without comment. The developer points it out, Claude fixes it, and then the same category of violation resurfaces an hour later in a different component. What would most reliably prevent this recurrence?
options: Restart the session every two hours to keep context "fresh"

Maintain a scratchpad file (e.g., a running constraints doc) recording critical architectural invariants as they're discovered, and have Claude reference it before generating new async code — giving the constraint a durable source of truth instead of relying on it staying salient in a long, growing conversation
Run a context-compaction command every hour regardless of what's happening
Ask Claude to restate the constraint out loud every 30 minutes
questions.explain:
A running scratchpad of architectural constraints, checked before generating new code in the affected area, gives a long session a durable place for a constraint to live outside the conversation's own "salience," which is what silently erodes as the session grows and moves on to new topics. Restarting periodically or compacting on a fixed schedule don't specifically preserve this kind of constraint — they just change what else gets lost along with it.
Not “Restart the session every two hours to keep context "fresh"” — Restarting every two hours loses the context built up and does not preserve the architectural constraint across the new session.
Not “Run a context-compaction command every hour regardless of what's ha…” — Compaction on a schedule can discard the constraint along with other detail, so it does not reliably keep it available.
Not “Ask Claude to restate the constraint out loud every 30 minutes” — Asking Claude to restate the rule periodically relies on the model recalling it, and a restatement does not give a durable source to check before writing code.

questions.q: A coordinator needs to explore two mutually exclusive research hypotheses at once: one line of investigation assuming "policy X accelerates adoption" and another assuming "policy X has no measurable effect." Using ordinary named subagents, each spawned fresh with only its own hypothesis in its prompt, the coordinator still finds that reasoning clearly built on one hypothesis leaks into the write-up for the other — findings that should only make sense under "accelerates" show up justifying "no effect" too. What's the most direct fix for exploring genuinely incompatible branches like this?
options: Add allowedTools: ["Task"] to the coordinator's configuration, since parallel spawn requires it

Fork the session at the point where the branches diverge, so each hypothesis is explored in its own isolated copy of the accumulated investigation state, then compare the two forks' conclusions afterward
Parallel Task calls cannot accept differing prompts; switch to strictly sequential delegation instead
Have the synthesis agent automatically detect and remove cross-hypothesis contamination after the fact
questions.explain:
Forking at the point where two genuinely incompatible investigations diverge gives each hypothesis its own isolated copy of the shared context to build on independently, preventing conclusions grounded in one hypothesis from leaking into the other's write-up. Ordinary fresh named subagents don't solve this on their own if the coordinator's framing or the shared setup still lets assumptions bleed across branches.
Not “Add allowedTools: ["Task"] to the coordinator's configuration, si…” — Adding Task to allowedTools only enables spawning subagents. It does nothing to stop one hypothesis's reasoning leaking into the other's write-up.
Not “Parallel Task calls cannot accept differing prompts; switch to st…” — Parallel Task calls can take different prompts, and sequential delegation would not isolate the branches from each other.
Not “Have the synthesis agent automatically detect and remove cross-hypo…” — Cleaning up contamination after the fact is unreliable. The branches should be separated from the moment they diverge.

questions.q: A coordinator delegates "research the EU's approach to a regulatory topic" to a named search subagent, and later delegates "research the US's approach to the same regulatory topic" to that same subagent. In between, the coordinator's own conversation has built up 15 turns of discussion establishing shared terminology and which document sources are authoritative for this topic. The second delegation comes back sparse and generic, as if the subagent doesn't share any of that established framing. What's the most accurate explanation?
options: Subagents automatically inherit the coordinator's full conversation history, so the sparseness must mean the second request itself was too narrow

A subagent only receives what's explicitly included in its own invocation prompt; context the coordinator built up in its own conversation — terminology, source guidance — isn't automatically available to a subagent unless the coordinator restates it in that subagent's prompt
The first delegation exhausted the subagent's usable sources, degrading the second
Subagents share a temporary memory keyed by topic, but that memory had already expired between the two delegations
questions.explain:
A subagent only has what's explicitly included in its own invocation prompt. Terminology and source guidance the coordinator built up in its own conversation over 15 turns doesn't automatically travel with a new delegation — it has to be restated in that subagent's prompt, which is exactly what was missing here.
Not “Subagents automatically inherit the coordinator's full conversation…” — Subagents do not inherit the coordinator's history. The sparse result points to missing context in the prompt, not a narrow request.
Not “The first delegation exhausted the subagent's usable sources, degra…” — Nothing suggests sources were exhausted. The result lacked the terminology and source guidance that was never passed in.
Not “Subagents share a temporary memory keyed by topic, but that memory …” — Subagents do not share a topic-keyed memory that expires, so there is no such store to blame for the generic answer.

questions.q: A synthesis agent constantly needs to fact-check small claims mid-report — "is 2023 the right year for that report," "did that agency actually issue this," "is this within the stated margin of error." Every check currently routes through the coordinator to a full-capability search subagent, adding a few seconds of round-trip latency each time, and the synthesis agent makes 80+ such checks per report. What tool-distribution change is most appropriate?
options: Give the synthesis agent unrestricted access to the same web-search and document-analysis tools the other subagents use

Give the synthesis agent one narrow, scoped tool built specifically for quick single-fact verification, so the common case resolves locally, while genuinely complex verification still routes through the coordinator
Batch all 80+ checks into one large request sent to the coordinator at the very end
Remove fact verification from the synthesis step entirely to save latency
questions.explain:
A narrow, purpose-built verification tool for simple single-fact checks lets the high-frequency, low-complexity case resolve locally without a coordinator round-trip, while genuinely complex verification still goes through the coordinator. Giving the synthesis agent full search/analysis tool access reintroduces the coordination and scope problems that scoped tools are meant to avoid.
Not “Give the synthesis agent unrestricted access to the same web-search…” — Unrestricted search access gives the synthesis agent tools outside its specialisation, which invites misuse and scope problems.
Not “Batch all 80+ checks into one large request sent to the coordinator…” — Batching 80+ checks to the end delays catching errors and does not remove the per-check round-trip cost during synthesis.
Not “Remove fact verification from the synthesis step entirely to save l…” — Removing fact checks to save time lets small factual errors through, trading accuracy for speed instead of making checks cheaper.

questions.q: A research pipeline runs parallel subagents, then sends their combined output straight to a report-writing step with no intermediate check. Reviewers later find citation mismatches (a claim attributed to one source that actually came from another) and outright contradictions between two sections of the same report. Every individual subagent's own output looks reasonable in isolation. Where is the defect, and what's the most effective fix?
options: One specific subagent must have misattributed a source; re-run that subagent with stricter instructions
The report-writing step is introducing the citation errors itself; add a citation-cleanup pass after report generation
Add an explicit coordinator-level checkpoint that evaluates the combined findings against citation-accuracy and cross-section-consistency criteria before handing off to report generation
The problem is in how tool responses format citations; normalize citation format with a hook
questions.explain:
Every subagent looking correct in isolation doesn't guarantee the combined output is coherent — that's exactly why an explicit checkpoint evaluating the aggregated findings against citation-accuracy and cross-section-consistency criteria, before report generation runs, catches problems that no individual subagent would ever surface on its own.
Not “One specific subagent must have misattributed a source; re-run that…” — Every subagent's output looks fine on its own, so nothing indicates one subagent misattributed a source. The problem appears only when results are combined.
Not “The report-writing step is introducing the citation errors itself; …” — The cleanup after report generation catches errors too late, and the mismatches arise from combining findings that were never checked together beforehand.
Not “The problem is in how tool responses format citations; normalize ci…” — Citation format normalisation addresses presentation, not whether claims are attributed to the right source or whether sections contradict each other.

questions.q: A coordinator launches three subagents in parallel — search, document analysis, and synthesis — for a request that fundamentally depends on reconciling conflicting findings across topics. Search and document analysis both succeed; synthesis crashes partway through with an unrecoverable internal error. The coordinator now has two successful results and one hard failure, for a task where the missing synthesis step was the part actually responsible for resolving the conflicts the user asked about. What should the coordinator do?
options: Always return the two successful results as a partial report, since some information is better than none

Reason about whether the failed piece was essential to what was actually asked — since here the synthesis step was the entire point (reconciling conflicts), a partial report without it would misrepresent the state of the research, so this case should escalate rather than quietly return partial output
Retry the synthesis step exactly once more and return whatever it produces, succeed or fail
Discard everything and start the whole three-subagent pipeline over
questions.explain:
The right call depends on whether the failed piece was essential to what was actually asked. Here, reconciling conflicts across topics was the entire point of the request, and synthesis was the step responsible for that — so a "successful" partial report from just search and document analysis would misrepresent whether the actual question got answered, and escalating is more honest than quietly returning an incomplete result.
Not “Always return the two successful results as a partial report, since…” — Returning a partial report without the reconciliation the user asked for would suggest the question was answered when it was not.
Not “Retry the synthesis step exactly once more and return whatever it p…” — One retry returning whatever happens does not account for whether the missing piece was essential, so a failed retry could still yield a misleading output.
Not “Discard everything and start the whole three-subagent pipeline over” — Discarding the successful search and analysis results wastes valid work, and restarting does not address whether the failure is recoverable.

questions.q: A document-analysis subagent is scoped to extract findings only from a fixed, pre-approved set of internal PDFs. To let it double-check facts against the source text, it's given general-purpose web-search access as well. Within weeks, logs show it routinely uses that web-search access to pull in and cite outside sources the coordinator never approved, expanding scope well past the original document set. What's the most direct fix?
options: Remove web search entirely and tell the subagent, via the system prompt, to rely only on the approved documents
Replace the general web-search tool with a narrowly scoped verification tool that can only check claims against the specific approved document set, not the open web
Add a stronger prompt warning against using search to expand scope
Let the coordinator strip out any external citations from the subagent's output after the fact
questions.explain:
The scope-creep problem is a tool-design problem, not a prompting problem: replacing general web search with a tool that can only verify claims against the already-approved document set makes scope expansion structurally impossible, rather than relying on the model to voluntarily stay within bounds it technically still has the power to exceed.
Not “Remove web search entirely and tell the subagent, via the system pr…” — Removing web search and relying on a prompt instruction still depends on the model complying, and it loses the ability to verify against the approved sources.
Not “Add a stronger prompt warning against using search to expand scope” — A stronger prompt warning is advisory only, so the subagent can still use general search to pull in outside sources.
Not “Let the coordinator strip out any external citations from the subag…” — Stripping citations afterward treats the symptom, since the subagent still uses unapproved material in its reasoning.

questions.q: A multi-day research session is interrupted right after the search subagent finishes but before document analysis begins. The team wants to resume without re-running search from scratch. They restart the coordinator, and it sends document analysis a fresh prompt describing the new task — but never tells it what search already found. What's the most maintainable way to resume this kind of interrupted pipeline?
options: Just resume and let document analysis redo any lookups it needs; some redundant work is an acceptable tradeoff

Have each subagent export its completed state to a known location as it finishes, and have the coordinator load a manifest of that state on resume, re-injecting whatever a subsequent step actually needs
Manually copy-paste the search subagent's raw output into every future prompt for the rest of the session
Discard everything from before the interruption and start the whole pipeline over
questions.explain:
Structured state exports plus a coordinator-loaded manifest on resume is the reliable crash/interruption-recovery pattern: each subagent's completed work is captured in a known location, and resuming means loading that manifest and re-injecting only what a subsequent step actually needs, rather than redoing work or manually threading raw output through every future prompt.
Not “Just resume and let document analysis redo any lookups it needs; so…” — Redoing lookups wastes time and may produce different results than the earlier search, which the user wanted to avoid repeating.
Not “Manually copy-paste the search subagent's raw output into every fut…” — Pasting raw output into every future prompt is manual, bloats context, and is easy to forget or get wrong.
Not “Discard everything from before the interruption and start the whole…” — Starting over throws away the completed search work, defeating the goal of resuming without rerunning it.

questions.q: A team completes a multi-day research project on a fast-moving regulatory topic, citing a dozen sources. Two weeks later, they resume the same line of research to expand on one sub-topic, and simply re-inject all the prior findings as-is into the new session before continuing. A week after publishing the expanded report, they learn that two of the originally-cited sources have since been formally retracted or substantially revised, and the report's now-outdated claims are actively misleading readers. What practice would have caught this before publication?
options: Store every source as a permanent, stable URL so readers can always find the original text themselves

When resuming research after a significant time gap, explicitly validate whether previously-cited sources are still current before re-using them, rather than re-injecting old findings wholesale and treating them as still authoritative
Have a policy of never citing anything more than six months old
Re-run the entire original research pipeline from scratch every time any new work touches the same topic
questions.explain:
Time-sensitive research doesn't stay valid forever; resuming after a real time gap and re-injecting old findings as if they're still current risks exactly this outcome — publishing on sources that have since been retracted or substantially revised. Explicitly validating source currency before reuse, rather than treating a prior session's findings as permanently authoritative, is what would have caught it.
Not “Store every source as a permanent, stable URL so readers can always…” — Stable URLs let readers find the original text but do not tell the team whether a cited source has since been retracted or revised.
Not “Have a policy of never citing anything more than six months old” — A fixed age cutoff is arbitrary. A recent source can be retracted, and an older one can still be valid.
Not “Re-run the entire original research pipeline from scratch every tim…” — Rerunning the whole pipeline each time is wasteful and does not specifically check whether earlier sources are still current.

questions.q: An agent explores a repository using an MCP tool for definition lookup and another for call-site discovery. Some calls fail during a long exploration session, and the integration currently returns every failure as {"isError": true, "message": "Tool unavailable"}, whether the cause is a transient network blip, a malformed query, or a rate limit. The agent retries every failure the same way, sometimes looping for a long time on a query that will never succeed no matter how many times it's retried. What must be added to the tool responses to fix the retry logic?
options: Raise the maximum retry count and add exponential backoff uniformly across all retried calls
Log additional detail in the failure message so a human can read it later
Add an errorCategory (e.g. transient / validation / permission) and an isRetryable boolean to each error response, so the agent can distinguish a worthwhile retry from a hopeless one
Remove the retry mechanism entirely and fail immediately on any error
questions.explain:
An errorCategory plus an isRetryable flag lets the agent tell a worthwhile retry (transient) apart from a hopeless one (a malformed query that will fail identically every time). Without that distinction, uniform retry logic burns time on exactly the calls retrying can never fix, and failing immediately on everything throws away the retries that would have actually succeeded.
Not “Raise the maximum retry count and add exponential backoff uniformly…” — More retries with uniform backoff would keep retrying calls that can never succeed, such as a malformed query, wasting time.
Not “Log additional detail in the failure message so a human can read it…” — A more readable message for a human does not give the agent a structured signal it can act on in its retry logic.
Not “Remove the retry mechanism entirely and fail immediately on any error” — Failing immediately on every error discards transient failures that would succeed on retry, so recoverable calls would be lost.

questions.q: A shared catalog of approved integrations (REST APIs, webhook destinations, supported SDK versions) is exposed as an MCP tool, list_integrations. During a typical 2-hour exploration session, the agent calls this tool 15+ times just to check what's available, and each call consumes a tool-use decision step even though the underlying list rarely changes within a session. What's the most efficient way to expose this catalog?
options: Merge several related discovery tools into one larger tool with a more detailed description
Cache the tool's output into CLAUDE.md so the agent can reference it as static project memory
Expose the integration catalog as an MCP **resource** rather than a tool, so it can be read directly without spending a tool-use decision each time
Add the integration list as literal text in the system prompt
questions.explain:
A catalog that's mostly static within a session and exists to be looked up, not acted on, is a textbook fit for an MCP resource — it can be read directly without spending a tool-use decision on every check. Caching into CLAUDE.md still requires a file read each time it's needed and goes stale silently; a single combined tool still costs a round trip per call.
Not “Merge several related discovery tools into one larger tool with a m…” — Merging discovery tools still costs a round trip per call, so the agent keeps spending decision steps on a static list.
Not “Cache the tool's output into CLAUDE.md so the agent can reference…” — A CLAUDE.md copy would need to be maintained by hand and goes stale silently when the catalogue changes, and it is not the natural mechanism for reference data.
Not “Add the integration list as literal text in the system prompt” — Hard-coding the list into the system prompt makes it static text that must be edited whenever it changes and bloats every request.

questions.q: During analysis, an agent needs the contents of three unrelated source files as baseline context before proposing any changes. It currently reads file A, waits for the result, reads file B, waits, then reads file C — three sequential tool-use round trips for three independent, non-dependent reads. What change improves efficiency here without changing what's actually being read?
options: Use a single Bash command to concatenate all three files with a shell glob instead of using the file-reading tool
Emit all three read calls together in one response, as separate tool-use blocks, so the client can execute them concurrently and return all three results at once
Split the analysis across three separate sessions, one file per session
Keep reading sequentially, but cache each file's contents locally to avoid reading it again later
questions.explain:
When several reads are genuinely independent of each other, emitting them together as separate tool-use blocks in one response lets the client run them concurrently and return all results at once, rather than paying three sequential round trips for work that never depended on being sequential in the first place.
Not “Use a single Bash command to concatenate all three files with a she…” — Using a shell command to concatenate files gives up the dedicated read tool and does not make the reads concurrent in the intended way.
Not “Split the analysis across three separate sessions, one file per ses…” — Spreading one analysis across three sessions fragments context, when the files are needed together as baseline context.
Not “Keep reading sequentially, but cache each file's contents locally t…” — Caching file contents does not remove the three sequential round trips for the first read of each independent file.

questions.q: One MCP database tool returns {"isError": true, "errorCategory": "transient", "isRetryable": true} on one call and {"isError": true, "errorCategory": "validation", "isRetryable": false} on a different call. If the agent's recovery logic treats every error identically and simply retries both the same way, what actually happens?
options: Both eventually succeed on retry; the transient one just takes a bit longer

The transient failure may well succeed on retry, but the validation failure (a malformed query, say) will keep failing identically every time, since retrying with the same bad input doesn't fix the input — wasting attempts and context on a call retrying can't help
Both fail regardless, and the agent should escalate both to a human immediately
Neither will ever succeed, so all retries should simply be disabled everywhere
questions.explain:
Treating every error identically wastes effort specifically on the validation failure, since retrying the same malformed input produces the same malformed result every time — only the transient failure has any real chance of resolving on retry. The fix isn't fewer or more retries across the board, it's recognizing which category is actually retryable.
Not “Both eventually succeed on retry; the transient one just takes a bi…” — If every failure is retried the same way, both would eventually be treated as recoverable, but the validation failure never succeeds because the input stays bad.
Not “Both fail regardless, and the agent should escalate both to a human…” — The transient failure may well succeed on retry, so both do not fail regardless. Treating both the same wastes effort on only one.
Not “Neither will ever succeed, so all retries should simply be disabled…” — Disabling retries everywhere throws away the transient case, which can succeed, so the answer is to distinguish categories.

questions.q: A developer-productivity agent has 22 tools available at once: 5 built-ins, 12 MCP tools for various kinds of code search (keyword search, cross-reference lookup, type-hierarchy exploration, and more), and 5 more for generating boilerplate. Logs show the agent occasionally reaches for a slower, more generic search tool when a faster, more specific one would clearly have been better — even after descriptions were already improved. What's the next lever to pull?
options: Cut the least-used tools until the total count is 10 or fewer
Switch to a model with a larger context window so tool-selection reasoning has more room

Narrow which tools are actually available per task type — e.g. an exploration-focused pass gets only a handful of high-signal search tools, while an implementation-focused pass gets the editing and boilerplate tools — reducing the live decision space itself rather than relying on ever-better descriptions alone
Build a separate preprocessing step that decides which tool to call before the agent ever sees the request
questions.explain:
Narrowing which tools are actually available for a given task phase reduces the live decision space itself, which is a more direct fix for misselection among 22 similar-looking tools than hoping ever-better descriptions alone will fully resolve it, or assuming a bigger context window somehow improves the underlying selection judgment.
Not “Cut the least-used tools until the total count is 10 or fewer” — Cutting to ten tools is arbitrary and removes capabilities the agent still needs, instead of narrowing the set for each task phase.
Not “Switch to a model with a larger context window so tool-selection re…” — A larger context window does not improve the agent's judgment in choosing between similar tools, so misselection would continue.
Not “Build a separate preprocessing step that decides which tool to call…” — A separate preprocessing step to pick tools adds a brittle routing layer, when scoping the tools available per phase is simpler.

questions.q: A system requires that all file modifications stay within an explicitly approved workspace_root directory. A developer asks an agent to "clean up unused dependencies," and without any programmatic boundary check in place, the agent occasionally ends up running Bash commands that touch directories outside that approved root. What is the most reliable way to enforce this boundary?
options: Add a hook that runs after the Bash command completes, checking whether it touched an out-of-scope path and rolling back if so
Have the agent itself run a path-check command before the real modification, as a self-imposed safeguard
Add a prompt instruction stating the boundary rule and monitor logs afterward for any violations
Add a hook that runs *before* the Bash tool executes, validates the target path against workspace_root, and blocks the command outright with feedback if it falls outside that boundary
questions.explain:
A hook that runs before the Bash tool executes and can validate the target path against workspace_root — blocking the call outright when it falls outside — is the only one of these options that can actually prevent an out-of-scope modification from happening. A post-hoc check or a self-imposed pre-check the agent might skip both allow the violation to occur first; a prompt instruction is advisory, not enforced.
Not “Add a hook that runs after the Bash command completes, checking whe…” — A check after the command finishes lets the out-of-scope modification happen first, and rolling back may not undo every side effect.
Not “Have the agent itself run a path-check command before the real modi…” — A self-imposed path check depends on the agent choosing to run it, so it can be skipped, which is the failure in the first place.
Not “Add a prompt instruction stating the boundary rule and monitor logs…” — A prompt rule with after-the-fact log monitoring is advisory, so violations still occur before anyone notices them.

questions.q: An MCP tool call returns an error with errorCategory: "permission". What does this most likely indicate, and what should the agent do next?
options: The operation timed out and will likely succeed if retried with backoff

The agent lacks sufficient authorization for this operation (missing credentials or an insufficient scope); retrying the same call won't change that outcome, so the right move is to escalate, request different credentials, or skip the operation rather than keep retrying
The input was malformed and should be reformatted before retrying
The operation actually succeeded, just with an empty result, and can be treated as a no-op
questions.explain:
A "permission" error category signals an authorization problem — missing credentials or an insufficient scope — which retrying the identical call will never resolve. The right response is to escalate, obtain different credentials, or skip the operation, not to keep retrying as if the failure might eventually clear on its own.
Not “The operation timed out and will likely succeed if retried with bac…” — A timeout is a transient failure that suits retry with backoff, whereas a permission error indicates the agent is not authorised.
Not “The input was malformed and should be reformatted before retrying” — A malformed input is a validation error. A permission error means authorisation is missing, so reformatting the input will not help.
Not “The operation actually succeeded, just with an empty result, and ca…” — A permission error is a failure, not a successful empty result, so treating it as a no-op would hide that the operation was blocked.

questions.q: A coordinator delegates codebase analysis across three subagents — one traces API handlers, one traces database writes, one analyzes tests — and each returns its findings as free-form prose summaries. When an implementation-focused step later tries to act on those summaries, it struggles to cite exact file paths, line numbers, or code snippets, since the prose only describes what was found in general terms. What change most improves reliability downstream?
options: Have the coordinator manually go back through the prose afterward and try to reconstruct file paths and line numbers from it
Reduce the number of subagents to one or two so there's less to reconcile

Require each subagent to return structured findings — the claim, the exact file path, a line range, and a short source excerpt — instead of unstructured prose, so precise attribution survives all the way through to the implementation step
Merge every subagent's findings into a single combined document and have the implementation step search for the referenced code itself
questions.explain:
Structured findings (claim, file path, line range, source excerpt) preserve exactly the precision that free-form prose summaries lose — without them, a later step has to try to reconstruct file-level detail from a paragraph that was never designed to carry it. Manually reconstructing that detail after the fact is error-prone and doesn't scale, and merging everything into one document doesn't restore detail that was never captured in the first place.
Not “Have the coordinator manually go back through the prose afterward a…” — Reconstructing file paths and line numbers from prose afterward is error-prone, and details that were never captured cannot be recovered reliably.
Not “Reduce the number of subagents to one or two so there's less to rec…” — Fewer subagents does not stop each from returning vague prose, so the downstream step would still lack exact locations.
Not “Merge every subagent's findings into a single combined document and…” — Combining everything into a single document and making the implementation step search again discards detail that the subagents already found.

questions.q: A team wants a slash command (skill) that only ever operates on files matching a specific pattern (e.g., generated API client files under a particular directory), regardless of which developer runs it or what else is open in their session. They configure this by adding disallowed-tools to the skill's own frontmatter to block file types outside that pattern. In testing, the command still successfully edits files outside the intended pattern when a developer runs it from a broader working context. What's actually going wrong?
options: disallowed-tools blocks entire tools (like Edit or Write) from being used at all — it has no concept of restricting a tool to only certain file paths, so it cannot enforce a pattern-based boundary on its own; a path-based restriction needs to be enforced elsewhere, such as through a hook that inspects the target path before allowing the edit
disallowed-tools only applies to MCP tools, never to built-in tools like Edit and Write
The command definition is being overridden by a broader project-level configuration every time
disallowed-tools requires an accompanying allowed-tools entry to take effect at all
questions.explain:
disallowed-tools operates at the level of whole tools, not individual file paths within a tool's use — it can prevent Edit from being used at all, but it has no mechanism for saying "only allow edits to files matching this pattern." Enforcing a path-based restriction requires something that actually inspects the target path before the edit happens, such as a hook, not a tool-level allow/deny list.
Not “disallowed-tools only applies to MCP tools, never to built-in tool…” — disallowed-tools is not limited to MCP tools and can block built-in tools. The problem is that it works at the level of whole tools.
Not “The command definition is being overridden by a broader project-lev…” — Nothing suggests a broader configuration is overriding the command. The behaviour follows from disallowed-tools having no concept of file path patterns.
Not “disallowed-tools requires an accompanying allowed-tools entry to…” — disallowed-tools does not need an accompanying allowed-tools entry. Even then it still could not restrict edits by path pattern.

questions.q: A developer-productivity agent needs to hand off from a broad, exploratory investigation phase to a narrow, high-precision code-modification phase for the same task, without losing the context gathered during exploration. Using two entirely separate agent definitions with no shared context would solve the tool-scoping problem but would also force the modification phase to start blind. What approach best preserves context while still narrowing tool access for the second phase?
options: Keep a single agent and rely on prompt instructions to describe which tools are appropriate for which phase, without changing what's actually available

Delegate the modification phase to a subagent that receives the exploration phase's key findings explicitly in its invocation prompt, and is scoped to a narrower toolset appropriate for making the actual edits — preserving continuity through the handoff while still tightening tool access for the higher-risk phase
Run the whole task in one phase with all tools available throughout, since narrowing access isn't worth the coordination overhead
Have the developer manually copy relevant findings into a new session before the modification phase begins
questions.explain:
Delegating the modification phase to a subagent that receives the exploration phase's key findings explicitly, while restricting its own toolset to what modification actually needs, preserves the continuity a fully separate, context-blind agent (the alternative being ruled out here) would lose, while still tightening tool access for the riskier, higher-precision phase.
Not “Keep a single agent and rely on prompt instructions to describe whi…” — Prompt instructions describing which tools to use do not change which tools are actually available, so the narrowing is not enforced.
Not “Run the whole task in one phase with all tools available throughout…” — Keeping all tools available throughout skips tightening access for the riskier modification phase, which is the aim.
Not “Have the developer manually copy relevant findings into a new sessi…” — Manually copying findings into a new session depends on the developer, risks omissions, and is far less reliable than an explicit handoff to a scoped subagent.

questions.q: A CI pipeline runs two independent jobs against the same PR: one does a general code review, the other runs a security-focused scan. Each spawns its own separate Claude Code invocation, and both happen to flag the same underlying issue (a missing null check on one specific line). Each job posts its own PR comment, so the same line gets two near-identical comments from two different "reviewers." Developers complain about the redundant notifications. What's the most effective way to prevent this specific kind of duplication?
options: Merge the two jobs into a single long-lived session so both sets of findings are produced together and can be reconciled before either is posted
Have whichever job runs second receive the first job's findings on the same PR as part of its input, with an instruction to skip anything the other job already flagged
Store every finding in a central datastore and run a deduplication pass across all findings from both jobs before anything is posted to GitHub
Force the two jobs to run strictly one after the other rather than in parallel, so the second can read a results file the first one wrote
questions.explain:
When two independent jobs can flag the same underlying issue, having the second job receive the first job's findings as input — with an explicit instruction to skip anything already flagged — removes the duplication at the source. Merging the jobs into one long-lived session creates the same kind of context-carryover risk seen elsewhere in CI reviews, and a purely infrastructure-level dedup pass is a heavier solution than simply passing the first job's output forward.
Not “Merge the two jobs into a single long-lived session so both sets of…” — Merging the jobs into one long-lived session allows context carryover between the general and security reviews and loses their independence.
Not “Store every finding in a central datastore and run a deduplication …” — A central datastore with a dedup pass is a heavier infrastructure approach than passing the first job's findings to the second.
Not “Force the two jobs to run strictly one after the other rather than …” — Forcing sequential runs alone does not stop duplicates unless the second job is told what the first already reported.

questions.q: A test-generation step produces unit tests referencing a fixture path like /opt/ci-fixtures/seed-data.json. These tests pass on every developer's local machine, but roughly 60% of them fail once run inside the containerized CI runner, where that absolute path doesn't exist. What's the most likely root cause, and the most direct fix?
options: The generated code assumes Unix-style paths; rewriting the tests to use Windows-style paths would resolve the CI failures

The test-generation prompt was never told that fixture paths must be relative to the repository root, and the project's CLAUDE.md doesn't document the test fixtures, helper utilities, or test-data layout actually available in the CI environment — so generation has no way to know the local absolute path won't exist there
CI containers mount volumes differently than developer machines; the fix belongs in the container configuration, not the generated tests
The test-generation step runs with context: fork, which is why it can't see the rest of the repository
questions.explain:
The generated tests fail in CI specifically because nothing available to the test-generation step describes the CI environment's actual fixture layout — the model has no way to know a developer-machine absolute path won't exist inside the container. Documenting the real fixture locations, helper utilities, and test-data structure in CLAUDE.md (or an equivalent always-loaded reference) gives every future invocation the information it's currently missing.
Not “The generated code assumes Unix-style paths; rewriting the tests to…” — The failure comes from the fixture path not existing in the container, not from Unix versus Windows path style.
Not “CI containers mount volumes differently than developer machines; th…” — Container mounts may differ, but the missing piece is that generation was never told the real fixture layout, which is why tests assume a local path.
Not “The test-generation step runs with context: fork, which is why it…” — context: fork is not shown to be involved. The tests fail because nothing documents the CI environment's fixtures for generation.

questions.q: A code-review job outputs structured findings (line_number, severity, description) via enforced JSON schema output. Reviewing a sample of findings, several reference line numbers well outside the actual range of lines the PR touched — for example, a finding at line 287 on a PR that only modified lines 42–156. These out-of-range findings still get posted as PR comments, where they read as irrelevant noise. What's the most reliable way to stop out-of-bounds findings from being posted?
options: Add an instruction to the review prompt: "only report findings within the changed lines of the diff"
Before posting each finding as a comment, validate its line_number against the PR diff's actual line range, and discard (or hold for manual review) anything that falls outside it
Switch to a larger model on the theory that it will have a better understanding of file scope
Lower the sampling temperature so line numbers come out "more precise"
questions.explain:
A prompt instruction to "only report changed lines" doesn't stop the model from generating a line number outside that range in the first place; validating each finding's line_number against the PR's actual diff bounds before posting is the deterministic check that actually filters out-of-range findings, rather than hoping instruction-following prevents them.
Not “Add an instruction to the review prompt: "only report findings with…” — A prompt instruction does not stop the model from emitting an out-of-range line number, so such findings can still appear.
Not “Switch to a larger model on the theory that it will have a better u…” — A larger model can still produce line numbers outside the diff, and it offers no deterministic guarantee that findings stay in range.
Not “Lower the sampling temperature so line numbers come out "more precise"” — Lower temperature affects randomness but does not bind the model to the diff's line range, so it cannot guarantee in-range findings.

questions.q: A .claude/rules/security.md file scoped with paths: ["src/**/*.ts"] contains guidance like "wrap all async operations in try/catch." Applied uniformly, this guidance also fires on test files such as src/auth.test.ts, where patterns like expect(promise).rejects.toThrow() are the idiomatic way to test a rejection and genuinely don't need a surrounding try/catch. Developers have started dismissing these findings as "doesn't apply to tests." What's the best way to separate production guidance from test-file guidance here?
options: Add an informal exception clause directly into the security guidance's prose: "...except in test files"

Add a second rule file scoped to test files specifically (e.g. paths: ["src/**/*.test.ts"]) containing test-aware guidance, so test files get conventions appropriate to tests instead of inheriting production-oriented rules wholesale
Remove all path-scoped rules and rely solely on a single root-level project memory file for every convention
Turn the security guidance off entirely until someone manually reviews every future finding
questions.explain:
A second rule file scoped specifically to test files lets test-appropriate conventions apply on their own terms, instead of inheriting a production-oriented rule (like mandatory try/catch wrapping) that doesn't fit idiomatic test patterns such as asserting on a rejected promise. This is more maintainable than an informal prose exception bolted onto the production rule, and it doesn't require giving up path-scoped guidance altogether.
Not “Add an informal exception clause directly into the security guidanc…” — A prose exception bolted onto the production rule is informal, can be ignored, and keeps test files inheriting guidance that does not fit them.
Not “Remove all path-scoped rules and rely solely on a single root-level…” — Removing path-scoped rules would lose the ability to apply conventions by file type, and a single root file brings back the bloat.
Not “Turn the security guidance off entirely until someone manually revi…” — Turning off the guidance gives up useful production checks entirely instead of separating the rules by file type.

questions.q: A test-generation prompt says "write thorough unit tests," and the resulting tests assert on implementation details — e.g. checking that a specific internal helper function was called a specific number of times — rather than on observable outcomes. The tests pass initially, but as soon as the implementation is reorganized (with identical external behavior), they break, generating churn complaints even though nothing user-facing changed. The prompt already includes "focus on behavior." What's the most effective next step?
options: Lower max_tokens to force shorter, and hopefully simpler, tests
Provide 2–3 concrete before/after examples contrasting an implementation-detail test with a behavior-driven test for the same function, and document the distinction as a standard in CLAUDE.md
Switch to a larger model, expecting it to have an inherently better grasp of testing philosophy
Have developers manually rewrite every generated test to remove implementation-detail assertions
questions.explain:
"Focus on behavior" alone hasn't resolved the ambiguity because "behavior" itself needs to be pinned down concretely; before/after examples contrasting an implementation-detail assertion with a behavior-driven one, documented as a standard, gives the model a concrete boundary to apply consistently — which a vague prose instruction, a smaller max_tokens budget, or a different model don't provide on their own.
Not “Lower max_tokens to force shorter, and hopefully simpler, tests” — max_tokens limits output length and does not tell the model to assert on outcomes rather than on internals, so tests stay brittle.
Not “Switch to a larger model, expecting it to have an inherently better…” — A larger model does not define what behaviour means for this codebase, so the ambiguity that produced the brittle tests would remain.
Not “Have developers manually rewrite every generated test to remove imp…” — Manually rewriting every generated test removes the automation benefit instead of fixing what the generator is told.

questions.q: A test-generation step is given the existing test file as context specifically to avoid creating duplicate tests. It still generates a new test with the exact same name as an existing one in that file — both are named identically. When the suite runs, the second definition silently overwrites the first, and the original test never executes again without anyone noticing. What's the most direct fix?
options: Run the test-generation step multiple times and have a developer manually reconcile any conflicts
Adopt a policy requiring every test name in the codebase to be globally unique, enforced by developer discipline
Include an explicit list of the existing test names already present in that file as part of the context, with an instruction to avoid reusing any of them
Disable test generation entirely for any file that already has existing tests
questions.explain:
The generation step already had the existing test file as context, but nothing told it those exact names were already taken; explicitly listing the existing test names and instructing the model to avoid reusing any of them gives it the specific information needed to prevent a silent, accidental name collision.
Not “Run the test-generation step multiple times and have a developer ma…” — Running generation repeatedly and having a developer reconcile conflicts adds manual work and still lets silent name collisions slip through.
Not “Adopt a policy requiring every test name in the codebase to be glob…” — A globally unique naming policy that relies on developer discipline is unenforced, and it does not give the generation step the names it must avoid.
Not “Disable test generation entirely for any file that already has exis…” — Disabling generation for files that already have tests loses valuable new coverage rather than just avoiding name collisions.

questions.q: A PostToolUse hook runs a code formatter after every file write, keeping the repository consistently formatted. A code-review job separately reads source files to analyze them and produce line-numbered findings as JSON. Because the review job's own file reads don't trigger the formatter, that's not the issue — instead, a separate process reformats the PR's files as part of an unrelated pre-review step, and the review job's line numbers, computed after that reformatting, no longer line up with the original PR diff's line numbers. Posted comments end up pointing at the wrong lines. What's the underlying issue, and the fix?
options: The review job should read from a snapshot of the files exactly as they existed in the PR diff, before any reformatting step touches them, so its line numbers stay aligned with what reviewers actually see in the diff
The formatter is changing line counts when it shouldn't; configure it to never alter line counts, even when reformatting
This is expected and unavoidable; the review prompt should instruct the model to guess at likely line-number drift
