The review job needs a larger context window so it can somehow account for the reformatting on its own
questions.explain:
Once a separate process reformats the PR's files before review reads them, any line numbers the review computes are aligned to the reformatted version, not to the diff reviewers are actually looking at. Reading from a snapshot taken before that reformatting step keeps the review's line numbers aligned with the PR diff itself, which is what the posted comments need to match.
Not “The formatter is changing line counts when it shouldn't; configure …” — Forcing the formatter to preserve line counts is impractical and only addresses the symptom. The review should read the files as they appear in the diff.
Not “This is expected and unavoidable; the review prompt should instruct…” — Guessing at line-number drift is unreliable. The fix is to read from the original pre-reformatting version so the numbers match.
Not “The review job needs a larger context window so it can somehow acco…” — Window size has no effect on offsets introduced by an external reformatting step, so the line numbers would still be misaligned.

questions.q: A code-review tool call returns findings with fields including finding_type (an enum: bug / style / performance / security) and description (free text). Every finding passes schema validation — the JSON is well-formed and every field has a legal value. But some findings are miscategorized: a finding with finding_type: "security" has a description reading "variable naming could be more concise," which is clearly a style comment, not a security issue. This routes the finding to the wrong downstream review queue, and schema validation doesn't catch it. What's the most reliable fix?
options: Add more fine-grained values to the finding_type enum to reduce ambiguity between categories
Add a deterministic post-generation check that cross-references finding_type against keyword/pattern signals in description, flagging likely category mismatches before the finding is routed anywhere
Switch to a larger model on the assumption it will have better categorical judgment
Lower max_tokens to encourage more concise, and hopefully more accurate, categorization
questions.explain:
Schema validation only confirms the JSON is well-formed and each value is a legal enum member — it has no way to check whether the chosen category actually matches the finding's own description. A deterministic post-generation check that cross-references category against description content catches exactly this class of semantically-wrong-but-syntactically-valid output, which more enum granularity or a different model wouldn't reliably fix.
Not “Add more fine-grained values to the finding_type enum to reduce a…” — More enum values do not check that the chosen category matches the description, so a finding could still be labelled wrongly.
Not “Switch to a larger model on the assumption it will have better cate…” — A larger model may reduce mistakes but cannot guarantee correct categorisation, whereas a deterministic check catches mismatches reliably.
Not “Lower max_tokens to encourage more concise, and hopefully more ac…” — max_tokens limits length and has no effect on whether a category matches the finding's description.

questions.q: A test-generation job runs in a completely fresh session for each PR, producing tests that technically pass locally but consistently fail once merged into the team's CI suite — because they use generic ad hoc mocking instead of the repository's established test harness, custom fixtures, and helper utilities. The invocation only receives the changed code; none of the team's testing conventions or available utilities are documented anywhere the generation step can see them. What combination of changes would most improve generated test quality here?
options: Move testing guidance to an external wiki that developers are expected to read themselves; tests will improve once humans internalize the conventions

Document the team's testing conventions, available fixtures/helpers, and test-harness setup in CLAUDE.md so every test-generation invocation has that context available, and include a short example showing correct use of the existing test infrastructure
Restrict test generation to only the simplest, dependency-free utility functions
Stop using Claude Code for test generation on anything that depends on shared test infrastructure
questions.explain:
The generated tests fail in CI because nothing in the invocation describes the team's actual test infrastructure; documenting conventions, fixtures, and helpers in CLAUDE.md (giving every invocation that context) combined with a concrete example of correct usage (showing, not just telling, what "correct" looks like) directly targets the missing information, rather than relying on developers to catch it after the fact or restricting generation to only the simplest possible cases.
Not “Move testing guidance to an external wiki that developers are expec…” — An external wiki depends on humans reading it and is invisible to the test-generation step, so the generated tests keep using generic mocking.
Not “Restrict test generation to only the simplest, dependency-free util…” — Restricting generation to simple dependency-free functions avoids the problem instead of fixing it, and gives up useful coverage.
Not “Stop using Claude Code for test generation on anything that depends…” — Abandoning generation for code that uses shared infrastructure gives up value when the real fix is to document the infrastructure.

questions.q: An invoice-extraction pipeline using tool_use with a strict JSON schema produces syntactically valid JSON every time, but a downstream review flags that a vendor_name value like "Acme Corp" sometimes appears in the output even though no such name exists anywhere in the source document. The schema defines vendor_name as a required string. What change would most reliably catch this kind of hallucination going forward?
options: Lower the temperature to force more deterministic output
Make vendor_name nullable instead of required

Add a vendor_source_location field (e.g., "letterhead," "signature block," "table header," or null) documenting where in the source the vendor name was actually found, forcing the extraction to ground its claim in something checkable
Add a few-shot example that explicitly instructs the model not to hallucinate
questions.explain:
Schema validity only confirms the JSON is well-formed, not that a claimed value actually exists in the source. A vendor_source_location field forces the extraction to ground its claim in a specific, checkable part of the document — a null value there signals the vendor genuinely wasn't found, making hallucination visible in a way a required-but-ungrounded string field never was.
Not “Lower the temperature to force more deterministic output” — Lower temperature does not tie the value to the document, so the model can still output a name that never appears in the source.
Not “Make vendor_name nullable instead of required” — Making vendor_name nullable removes the pressure to invent a value but does not let you verify that a non-null value actually appears in the source.
Not “Add a few-shot example that explicitly instructs the model not to h…” — An example telling the model not to hallucinate is a probabilistic instruction, so it does not give a checkable guarantee.

questions.q: A contract-extraction pipeline has two tools: one for prose clauses, one for tabular terms. Many real contracts contain both. The two tool descriptions currently say one extracts "contract text" and the other extracts "document tables," but in practice the model tends to call only one of the two tools even on documents that clearly contain both prose and tables. What's the most direct fix?
options: Merge the two tools into a single combined extraction tool
Rewrite both descriptions to clearly state which data each tool covers, and explicitly note that documents containing both prose and tables should trigger both tools in sequence
Force tool_choice to a single specific named tool
Add a preprocessing step that physically splits every document into separate table-only and prose-only files before extraction
questions.explain:
Tool descriptions are the primary signal driving selection; when they're vague about scope and silent on documents that need both tools, the model has no reason to call more than one. Making the descriptions explicit about what each covers — and stating outright that a document with both prose and tables should trigger both — directly addresses the observed under-calling, ahead of merging the tools or forcing a single named tool.
Not “Merge the two tools into a single combined extraction tool” — Merging the tools hides the distinction between prose and tables and does not fix the underlying issue, which is unclear descriptions.
Not “Force tool_choice to a single specific named tool” — Forcing one specific tool would guarantee the other is never called, making under-extraction worse.
Not “Add a preprocessing step that physically splits every document into…” — Splitting every document into table-only and prose-only files adds a complicated preprocessing step when clearer descriptions would solve it.

questions.q: A team processes 40 vendor invoices as a single long batch within one conversation. The first 10 or so extract cleanly, but starting partway through the batch, later invoices begin returning vendor names, account numbers, or reference codes that actually belong to an earlier invoice in the same batch, not the one currently being extracted. What change would most reliably eliminate this cross-document carryover?
options: Increase max_tokens to give the model more room to extract carefully
Split the batch into independent single-invoice extraction calls instead of processing all 40 within one shared conversation
Add a scratchpad listing every vendor and reference number seen so far, instructing the model to avoid reusing any value already on the list
Lower the model's temperature
questions.explain:
Processing all 40 invoices inside one shared conversation lets details from earlier documents bleed into later extractions as context accumulates — splitting the batch into independent, single-invoice calls removes the shared context that's causing the carryover entirely, rather than just narrowing it (as a scratchpad, C, would) or hoping more tokens or a lower temperature changes the underlying behavior.
Not “Increase max_tokens to give the model more room to extract carefully” — max_tokens limits output length and does not stop earlier invoices' details from bleeding into later extractions.
Not “Add a scratchpad listing every vendor and reference number seen so …” — A list of values seen so far only narrows the problem and grows with the batch, while the shared accumulating context remains.
Not “Lower the model's temperature” — Lower temperature does not remove the shared conversation context that is causing earlier invoices to affect later ones.

questions.q: A purchase-order extraction schema requires a po_number field and also has a document_type enum ("purchase_order" | "invoice" | "quote"). In practice, many documents get classified as "purchase_order" even though they're actually invoices that never contained a PO number at all — and validation, which runs only after the full extraction is returned, then fails on the missing po_number. What change would most reliably improve accuracy here?
options: Keep retrying the same prompt until validation happens to pass
Make po_number nullable so invoices no longer fail validation, while keeping document_type required as-is
Restructure extraction into two steps: first classify the document type from its structure/headers, then only require po_number when that first step actually confirms the document is a purchase order
Drop the po_number requirement from the schema entirely
questions.explain:
Since whether po_number should even be expected depends entirely on the document actually being a purchase order, classifying the document type first and only then conditionally requiring po_number prevents the mismatch from ever reaching validation, instead of discovering it only after the full extraction already ran or giving up the requirement across the board.
Not “Keep retrying the same prompt until validation happens to pass” — Retrying the same prompt does not fix a misclassified document, and a retry could just fail the same way repeatedly.
Not “Make po_number nullable so invoices no longer fail validation, wh…” — Making the field nullable removes the validation failure but does not fix the misclassification of invoices as purchase orders.
Not “Drop the po_number requirement from the schema entirely” — Dropping po_number entirely loses the field for documents that really are purchase orders.

questions.q: A contract-extraction schema has a required contract_start_date field. Some contracts state both an "executed date" (when the parties signed) and a separate "effective date" (when obligations actually begin), and these differ. The model picks inconsistently between the two across otherwise-similar contracts, and adding a couple of generic few-shot examples hasn't resolved the inconsistency. What's the next step?
options: Increase max_tokens to give the model more room to reason about which date to pick
Merge both dates into a single freeform text field instead of picking one

Add few-shot examples that include the explicit reasoning for the choice (e.g., "when both dates appear, prefer the effective date, since that's when obligations actually begin") plus a schema-level comment stating that precedence rule directly
Switch to a larger model and hope it infers the right precedence on its own
questions.explain:
Generic before/after examples weren't enough because they didn't convey *why* one date should be preferred over the other; adding the explicit precedence reasoning to the examples, backed by a schema-level comment stating the same rule, gives the model a concrete, repeatable basis for the choice instead of leaving it to infer a pattern from examples alone.
Not “Increase max_tokens to give the model more room to reason about w…” — More max_tokens allows longer output but does not tell the model which date should take precedence.
Not “Merge both dates into a single freeform text field instead of picki…” — A free-text field combining both dates loses the structured start date that the schema needs and does not resolve which one counts.
Not “Switch to a larger model and hope it infers the right precedence on…” — A larger model has no way of knowing the team's precedence rule unless it is stated, so inconsistency may persist.

questions.q: Two extraction tools, one for pulling out defined terms from a contract and one for pulling out the parties' actual obligations, both currently have descriptions that vaguely claim to cover "important contract terms." Developers have observed that the terms-extraction tool is sometimes relied on to also capture obligations, leading to silently incomplete extractions when it doesn't. What's the most effective first fix?
options: Rewrite both descriptions to explicitly separate their scope — state precisely what each tool does and doesn't cover, with a short example for each, so the overlap in "important contract terms" no longer blurs the boundary
Force the pipeline to always call both tools on every document regardless of content
Merge the two tools into a single combined extraction tool
Add a validation check after extraction that tries to detect whether obligations are missing from the output
questions.explain:
Both tools currently describe themselves with the same vague phrase ("important contract terms"), which is exactly what's letting one substitute for the other. Rewriting the descriptions to state precisely what each does and doesn't cover, with an example apiece, removes the ambiguity directly — well ahead of forcing both tools to always run or merging them outright, which gives up the distinction the team wants to keep.
Not “Force the pipeline to always call both tools on every document rega…” — Always calling both tools wastes effort on documents that only need one, and it does not clarify what each covers.
Not “Merge the two tools into a single combined extraction tool” — Merging the tools gives up the distinction the team wants between defined terms and obligations.
Not “Add a validation check after extraction that tries to detect whethe…” — A check after extraction detects missing obligations late and does not fix the ambiguous descriptions causing the substitution.

questions.q: A team processes 500 supplier invoices every business day and wants to move extraction to the Message Batches API to capture a meaningful cost discount. Current same-day processing takes about 2 hours from submission. Downstream financial-close processes need results by 9 AM the next business day. The Batches API carries no latency SLA and can, in the worst case, take up to 24 hours. If a batch is submitted at 6 PM, what's the latest it might reasonably return under that worst case, and what does that imply?
options: Always by 8 AM the next morning, so the move is safe as planned

As late as 6 PM the following day (24 hours after submission) in the worst case — which would blow past the 9 AM downstream deadline entirely, meaning this workflow shouldn't rely on the Batches API for its full volume without a real fallback plan
Within roughly 2 hours, the same as the current synchronous process
There's a documented, guaranteed 18-hour turnaround specifically for financial workloads
questions.explain:
With no latency SLA, a 6 PM submission could in the worst case take the full 24 hours, landing right around 6 PM the following day — well past the 9 AM downstream deadline. Treating "up to 24 hours" as if it were a guaranteed same-morning turnaround or assuming it behaves like the current 2-hour synchronous process both mistake an unbounded worst case for a reliable one.
Not “Always by 8 AM the next morning, so the move is safe as planned” — There is no guarantee of an overnight finish. Without a latency SLA, a batch submitted at 6 PM could take much longer than until 8 AM.
Not “Within roughly 2 hours, the same as the current synchronous process” — Batch processing does not behave like the current synchronous process, and its completion time is not bounded by two hours.
Not “There's a documented, guaranteed 18-hour turnaround specifically fo…” — The Batches API has no documented guaranteed turnaround for financial or any other workloads, only a worst-case window.

questions.q: A vendor-management schema classifies every vendor with an enum: "supplier" | "contractor" | "service_provider" | "reseller". In practice, some real vendor relationships (joint ventures, co-managed partnerships, regional distributor arrangements) don't cleanly fit any of the four categories, and the model is forced into a misclassification every time one comes up. What schema change best handles this kind of long-tail extensibility?
options: Drop the enum constraint entirely and make vendor_category a free-text string
Add an "other" value to the enum, plus an optional vendor_category_detail string field for a free-text explanation whenever "other" is chosen
Create an entirely separate extraction tool for every additional vendor type as it's discovered
Add a confidence score to the category field and route anything below a threshold to manual review, without changing the enum itself
questions.explain:
An "other" enum value paired with a free-text detail field lets the schema stay structured and queryable for the common cases while still accommodating the genuine long tail of relationships that don't fit any predefined category — without either abandoning structure entirely or requiring a brand-new tool every time a new edge case appears.
Not “Drop the enum constraint entirely and make vendor_category a free…” — Dropping the enum for free text loses the structure and consistency of a fixed set, making categories harder to query and compare.
Not “Create an entirely separate extraction tool for every additional ve…” — Creating a new tool for every extra vendor type does not scale and means rewriting the pipeline repeatedly for edge cases.
Not “Add a confidence score to the category field and route anything bel…” — Routing low-confidence results to manual review leaves the enum unable to represent these relationships, so misclassifications continue.

questions.q: Six months into production, a team wants to analyze why certain extractions get rejected by downstream reviewers. Current logs record only document_id, field_name, extracted_value, and a final disposition of accepted or rejected — nothing about the document itself. The team suspects failures cluster around things like poor-quality scans, handwritten amounts, very long multi-page contracts where key terms appear late in the document, or particular vendor formats, but the existing logs give no way to confirm or prioritize any of that. What should be added to enable real root-cause analysis?
options: A random UUID per extraction, purely for tracing a record back to its source document

Structured document metadata logged alongside each extraction — source type (scanned vs. native), an OCR-quality signal where applicable, page count, and roughly where in the document the field was found — so rejections can be correlated with the actual characteristics of the input that produced them
A separate machine-learning model trained specifically to predict which documents are likely to fail
A recurring manual review of a random sample of rejections, done by hand, to look for patterns
questions.explain:
Logging the actual characteristics of the input alongside each extraction — scan quality, page count, roughly where in the document a field was found — is what makes it possible to correlate rejections with real causes (a long contract, a poor scan, a particular vendor's layout) instead of treating every rejection as an undifferentiated data point with nothing to explain it.
Not “A random UUID per extraction, purely for tracing a record back to i…” — A random UUID lets you trace a record back to its document, but says nothing about the document's characteristics that might explain rejections.
Not “A separate machine-learning model trained specifically to predict w…” — Training a separate prediction model is heavy and premature when basic input characteristics have not even been logged yet.
Not “A recurring manual review of a random sample of rejections, done by…” — Reviewing a random sample by hand is slow and does not scale, and without recorded input characteristics there is little to correlate.
